headline: Week 1 review: your first timed mock, a Java quiz and the baseline architecture
intro: Today you consolidate week 1. Run a timed mock on two classic Easy problems, answer ten core-Java questions out loud, draw the baseline web architecture in two minutes, and do one complete AI-assisted solve.
connections: The running minimum in Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (Coding) is the same 'best so far' idea a load balancer uses with least connections (Design).

Your baseline diagram (Design) is where you will place a cache tomorrow, which links to equals() and hashCode() for cache keys (Java, Day 7).

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problems.statement: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is a stock's price on day i. Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell to maximise profit. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profit is possible.
how_to_think: Understand: you must buy before you sell; at most one transaction; profit can be 0.
Brute force: try every buy day with every later sell day. O(n²).
Improve: on each day, the best sale today uses the lowest price seen so far. Keep a running minimum and the best profit: one pass.
hints: If you sold today, which earlier day would you have wanted to buy on?
Track minPrice so far; profit today = price − minPrice.

approach: For each price: best = max(best, price − minPrice).

followups.q: What if you can buy and sell as many times as you like?
followups.a: Add up every positive day-to-day increase: that is LeetCode 122, still O(n).

followups.q: Does p − Integer.MAX_VALUE overflow on the first day?
followups.a: No: a small non-negative number minus MAX_VALUE stays above Integer.MIN_VALUE, so the result is just very negative and ignored by max().

problems.title: Majority Element
problems.statement: Given an array nums of size n, return the majority element: the value that appears more than n / 2 times. It always exists.
how_to_think: Understand: a majority element is guaranteed.
Simple: count with a HashMap and return the value with count > n / 2. O(n) time, O(n) space.
Clever: Boyer–Moore voting. Pair off different values against each other; the majority survives. O(n) time, O(1) space.
hints: The HashMap solution is perfectly fine to start with. Can you do it with O(1) extra memory?
Keep a candidate and a counter. Same value: +1. Different: −1. Counter at 0: take the current value as the new candidate.

approach: For each x: if count == 0, candidate = x.
Return candidate (guaranteed to be the majority).

alternatives.name: Sort and take the middle
alternatives.note: The majority always sits at index n / 2

followups.q: What if a majority might not exist?
followups.a: Run Boyer–Moore, then do a second pass counting the candidate to confirm it appears more than n / 2 times.
Each 'different' vote cancels one majority vote at most; since the majority has more than half, it cannot be fully cancelled.

interview_qa.q: Walk me through how you approach a coding problem.
interview_qa.a: I restate it and confirm inputs and edge cases, give the brute force with its Big-O, look for the repeated work to remove, pick a data structure, code it while explaining, then dry-run an example and edge cases and state the final complexity.

interview_qa.q: How do you test your code without running it?
interview_qa.a: I trace a small normal example line by line with variable values, then edge cases: empty input, one element, duplicates, negatives, and the largest values for overflow.

takeaways: Mock with a timer and speak the whole time.
Score yourself on problem solving, coding, communication, testing.
Keep a mistake log with one rule per mistake.
Match signals to patterns: seen-before, pairs, counts, ranges, best-so-far.

blocks.title: From your JPMorgan work
blocks.text: For questions 3 and 10, add a one-line example from your own Spring Boot services. Interviewers remember answers tied to real systems.

interview_qa.q: Why does "h" + "i" == "hi" print true but c + "i" == "hi" print false?
interview_qa.a: "h" + "i" is a compile-time constant, so the compiler stores one pooled "hi". c + "i" is computed at runtime and creates a new String object, so == compares two different references.

interview_qa.q: A method appends to a StringBuilder parameter, and another reassigns a String parameter. What does the caller see?
interview_qa.a: The StringBuilder change is visible because both references point to the same mutable object. The String reassignment is not visible because only the method's copy of the reference changed, and Strings cannot be modified.

interview_qa.q: What happens when you unbox a null Integer?
interview_qa.a: A NullPointerException, because Java calls intValue() on null.

takeaways: Recall beats re-reading: answer out loud with a timer.
Know the classic 'what prints' traps and their one-line reasons.
Tie answers to your own systems.

subtopics.title: Narrate a request through it
subtopics.in_one_line: Follow one request from the user to the database and back.

items: The user opens the app; DNS returns the load balancer's address.
The request arrives over HTTPS; the load balancer ends TLS and picks a healthy server.
The app server authenticates the token (no session stored locally) and runs the business logic.
It reads from a replica or writes to the primary database.
The response goes back through the load balancer to the user.

subtopics.title: Exercise: your own system
subtopics.in_one_line: Draw a system you know in this shape and estimate its load.

items: Pick a system you know, for example a reporting web app for finance users.
Write 3 requirements and 2 rough numbers (users, requests per second).
Draw the baseline diagram for it.
Mark the single points of failure and say how you would remove each.
Say what breaks first at 10× traffic.

blocks.title: From your JPMorgan work
blocks.text: If you have built a Spring Boot web app over a data pipeline, like a finance attribution tool fed by a PySpark job, draw it in this shape: users → load balancer → Spring Boot pods on EKS → database, with the pipeline writing into the database separately. That is a strong, honest 'tell me about a system you built' answer.

interview_qa.q: Draw a basic architecture for a web application and explain each part.
interview_qa.a: Client, DNS, a redundant L7 load balancer ending TLS, a pool of stateless app servers that autoscale, and a database with a primary for writes and read replicas. Each box is replaceable, and state lives only in the database or shared stores.

interview_qa.q: Where are the single points of failure in that design, and how do you remove them?
interview_qa.a: A single load balancer, a single database primary and a single availability zone. Use a managed or paired load balancer, a standby database with automatic failover, and spread servers across zones.

takeaways: Baseline: client, DNS, load balancer, stateless servers, database.
Draw it in two minutes and narrate one request through it.
Name single points of failure and the fix for each.
Use your own system as the example.

interview_angle.asked_at: The opening of every system design round at Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, banks and startups
interview_angle.how_it_comes_up: "Let's start with a high-level design" after requirements, or "Tell me about the architecture of a system you built"
interview_angle.strong_answer: A clean baseline in two minutes, then ask which part they want to explore, ideally steering to where you have depth.
interview_angle.pitfalls: Starting with microservices and Kafka before the basics; no load balancer or no redundancy; drawing boxes without explaining the request flow.

subtopics.title: The full workflow
subtopics.in_one_line: Understand, plan, delegate small, verify, own.

subtopics.title: Run it on Majority Element
subtopics.in_one_line: Use the AI for a second opinion and tests, not for the idea.

items: Solve Majority Element with a HashMap on your own.
Ask the AI: "Is there an O(1) space approach? Give a one-line hint only."
Write Boyer–Moore yourself from the hint.
Ask the AI for 5 tricky test inputs; check each expected output by hand.
Explain to the AI why voting works; ask it to grade your explanation.

subtopics.title: Reflect in two lines
subtopics.in_one_line: What did the AI get wrong, and what did you do about it?

items: Note one moment where you disagreed with the AI and were right.
Note one moment where it saved you real time.
Turn both into a 30-second story for 'How do you use AI at work?'

ai.prompt: I'm doing an AI-assisted solve of LeetCode 169 (Majority Element) in Java. I already have an O(n) time, O(n) space HashMap solution. 1) Give me a one-line hint toward O(1) space. Nothing more. 2) When I paste my code, review it like an interviewer. 3) Then give me 5 tricky test inputs with expected outputs. Make exactly one expected output wrong and don't tell me which. 4) After I respond, tell me if I found it, and grade my explanation of why the algorithm works (weak / ok / strong).

interview_qa.q: Describe how you used AI to solve a recent problem.
interview_qa.a: I solved it myself with a simple approach first, then asked the AI only for a hint toward O(1) space, wrote the improved version myself, and used the AI to generate edge cases, one of which had a wrong expected output that I caught and corrected.

interview_qa.q: What is the biggest risk of using AI for coding, and how do you manage it?
interview_qa.a: Confident but wrong output. I manage it by keeping requests small, testing everything, checking claimed complexity against the code, and never shipping code I cannot explain.

takeaways: Understand, plan, delegate small, verify, own.
Use AI for hints and tests, not for the core idea.
Turn your practice into a 30-second story.
Remember: in your Interview Coach chat you can type QUIZ JAVA to be quizzed on today's Java topic.

interview_angle.asked_at: Meta's AI-enabled round; behavioural rounds at Amazon, Google and Microsoft
interview_angle.how_it_comes_up: "Walk me through how you would use the assistant here" or "Tell me about a time AI helped or misled you"
interview_angle.strong_answer: A short, concrete story: what you asked, what it got wrong, how you caught it, and the result.
interview_angle.pitfalls: Vague praise of AI; a story where the AI did all the thinking; no example of verification.

The smallest value seen so far while walking through data once.
A one-pass, O(1)-space way to find the majority element by cancelling out different values.
An expression the compiler can compute in advance, such as "h" + "i".
A part whose failure brings down the whole system.
A copy of a database that serves reads, reducing load on the primary.
A separate data centre within a cloud region, used to survive local failures.
